title: Remember
hookLine: memory is a commandment in Judaism
carry: a memory that leads to doing

lines: A SONG, A SMELL, A HALLWAY.
cards: Can you order someone to remember? You can tell a person to stand up, sit down, be quiet. But memory seems to come and go on its own.
A song on the radio brings back a summer. A smell brings back a grandmother's hallway. Nobody commands that.
And yet the Torah does exactly this. Again and again, it doesn't say try to remember, or it would be nice to remember. It commands: remember.
In Hebrew, it's one word: zachor.

teach.h: REMEMBER THE SABBATH, TO KEEP IT.
teach.b: Zachor is the command form of the Hebrew verb for remembering. It sits right inside the Ten Commandments: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Notice what follows the remembering: to keep it.
Memory in the Torah isn't a mood. It leads somewhere. The pattern starts with God.

teach.h: GOD REMEMBERED NOAH, AND A WIND.
teach.b: In the flood story: "And God remembered Noah." Next comes a wind over the earth, and the waters begin to go down. When God remembers, something moves.
Remembering is the first half of an act.
Moses, near the end of his life, sings to the people: "Remember the days of old." Ask your father, he says, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will explain.
Memory isn't stored in a book alone; it's passed hand to hand. There's a harder zachor too.

Deuteronomy says: "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way as ye came forth out of Egypt." Amalek attacked the weak and weary at the back of the line, and the passage closes with "thou shalt not forget."
On the Sabbath before Purim, tradition reads those verses aloud in synagogue, and that Sabbath is called Shabbat Zachor.
Remembering there includes remembering cruelty, so as not to look away from it. The word carries all the way to now: in the Yizkor memorial prayers, in Holocaust remembrance, in yesterday's candle.
Shabbat, the road out of Egypt, the people who came before, what was done to the weak: in each, the Torah pairs remembering with doing. A memory that leads to doing.

how: Jews keep the command to remember through Shabbat, the Passover seder, the reading of the Amalek verses on Shabbat Zachor before Purim, Yizkor memorial prayers, yahrzeit candles and Holocaust remembrance.

o: remember: a command that leads memory into action
a memorial prayer said for the dead on holidays
the scroll of Esther read aloud on Purim

p: a wind, and the waters go down

s: in the Torah, only people remember; God never does
"And God remembered Noah", and the waters begin to go down.
zachor appears in the Ten Commandments, about the Sabbath
"Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."
the Amalek passage ends with permission to forget
it closes with "thou shalt not forget."

games.q: the flood has covered the earth. the text says God remembered Noah. what happens next?
o: nothing changes; the memory is enough.
a wind passes over the earth, and the waters begin to go down.
Noah is given a new set of laws at once.
games.why: a wind passes over the earth and the waters go down. in the Torah, remembering is the first half of an act.

practice: Let one memory rise: something an older person told you, or something you saw that you don't want lost. Hold it in detail, where you were, what the light was like, the words someone used.
Then ask it Moses's question: who told me this, and who will I tell? If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the people who handed it to you.

wordCard.voice: Zachor. Remember: the Torah's command, for Shabbat, for the days of old, for what was done to the weak, a memory that leads to action. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: remember! The command form, as in the Sabbath commandment.

carryVoice: Your line: a memory that leads to doing. That's what zachor asks. That's today, done.
